extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning proof techniques and mathematical writing (introductory discrete/transition-to-proof course)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for producing clear, correct mathematical proofs (direct, contrapositive, contradiction, case analysis) and for good mathematical writing in an introductory proofs course.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for Direct Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a conditional statement 'If P, then Q' start by assuming P and use logic/definitions to deduce Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example pattern used repeatedly: 'Suppose P. [use definitions and algebraic manipulation] Therefore Q.' Use clear declarations (e.g., 'By definition ... there is an integer d with ...'). Use separate lines for clarity, at least when learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for Contrapositive Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove 'If P, then Q' by proving the logically equivalent contrapositive '~Q => ~P'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard setup: 'Proof. Suppose ~Q. Therefore ~P. ■' Example: to show 'If P then Q' assume 'not Q' and deduce 'not P'. Do not confuse contrapositive with converse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline for Proof by Contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove a statement P by assuming ~P and deriving a contradiction C ∧ ~C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard setup: 'Proof. Suppose ~P. Therefore C ∧ ~C. ■' You may not know C at the start; do scratch work assuming ~P until you obtain an obvious contradiction. This method is logically valid because (~P) => (C ∧ ~C) is equivalent to P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case Analysis (Using Cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: When truth of a statement depends on separate possibilities, examine each case and prove the statement in all cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify natural partitioning (e.g., n even or odd). For each case, assume the case hypothesis and prove the conclusion. Examples: proving 1+(-1)^{2n-1} is a multiple of 4 by considering n even and n odd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating Similar Cases / Use of 'Without Loss of Generality'
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more cases are nearly identical, it is appropriate to do one case and indicate the other(s) are similar using 'Without loss of generality...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: Avoid abbreviating as 'WLOG' for transparency. Until more experienced, write out all cases even if similar. Example: parity proofs where swapping roles of m and n yields identical algebra.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving Equality by Double Inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: To show m = n, show m ≤ n and n ≤ m (or m < n and n < m as appropriate); then conclude equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy note: reasoning to prove m ≤ n may be different from that to prove n ≤ m; treat each direction separately and then combine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work Backwards to Find Strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: When a direct forward derivation is unclear, work backward from the desired conclusion to a statement that is obviously true, then reverse the steps in the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: to prove 2√(xy) < x + y, square both sides to obtain 4xy < (x+y)^2, manipulate to 0 < (x-y)^2, which is obviously true, then reverse steps and justify squaring (positivity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Definitions Explicitly (Existence Clauses)
rubrics_metrics.description: When using definitions that assert existence (e.g., divisibility, even/odd), explicitly state the existential witness and its domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: From 'a | b' write 'there is an integer d with b = a d' (explicitly 'for some integer d'). From 'x is even' write 'x = 2a for some a ∈ Z.' Avoid omitting 'for some integer c' which forces the reader to scan backwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain Logical Justification When Manipulating Expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Every algebraic manipulation or multiplication of an equation should be justified and its consequences noted (e.g., closure in Z, positivity when dividing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: From a-b = nk multiply both sides by (a+b) and note c(a+b) ∈ Z so n | (a^2 - b^2). When dividing both sides, ensure divisor is known positive/nonzero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use DeMorgan's Laws When Negating Compound Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: When working with negations of compound statements (especially in contrapositive proofs), apply DeMorgan's laws to convert negations of conjunctions/disjunctions correctly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Negating 'b|x and b|y' gives 'b∤x or b∤y' and must be handled casewise thereafter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Begin a Sentence with a Mathematical Symbol
rubrics_metrics.description: Never begin a sentence with a mathematical symbol because sentences begin with capital letters and symbols are case sensitive, causing ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern examples given: 'X is an integer...' is bad; prefer 'The set A is a subset of B.' or 'Since x is an integer, 2x+5 is an integer.'

rubrics_metrics.name: End Each Sentence with a Period
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when a sentence ends with a mathematical symbol or expression, end it with a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical statements are like English phrases containing special symbols, so use normal punctuation. Examples show Euler's formulas and how to punctuate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate Mathematical Symbols and Expressions with Words
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert words between mathematical symbols/expressions in prose to prevent distinct expressions from appearing to merge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'Because -1 = 0, :3c = 1 or :)c = -1.' Correct: 'Because x^2 - 1 = 0, it follows that x = 1 or x = -1.' Also separate set notation from prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Misuse of Symbols in Prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Symbols such as =, <, ∈ are not words and should not be used as substitutes for words outside mathematical expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: 'Since the two sets are =, one is a subset...' Correct: 'Since the two sets are equal, one is a subset of the other.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Using Unnecessary Symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not introduce unnecessary or redundant symbols; concise verbal expression is often clearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'No set X has negative cardinality.' Better: 'No set has negative cardinality.' Keep notation minimal unless needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use First Person Plural ('we')
rubrics_metrics.description: In mathematical writing, prefer 'we' and 'us' rather than 'I', 'you', or 'me' to create a conversational, guiding tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style suggestion to improve readability and inclusiveness of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer Active Voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the active voice to make mathematical writing more lively and direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'The value a = 3 is obtained through division...' Better: 'Dividing both sides by 5, we get x = 3.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain Each New Symbol When Introduced
rubrics_metrics.description: Every new symbol introduced in a proof must have its meaning explained to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: writing 'b = a c' without saying 'for some integer c.' Always state 'for some integer c' when invoking divisibility definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Ambiguous Pronouns (Watch Out for 'it')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use pronouns like 'it' when their antecedent could be unclear; instead name the object explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of 'we see that it is not empty', write 'we see that Y is not empty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Care with 'Since, because, as, for, so' (Implicit Assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using these conjunctions asserts that the antecedent P is true in addition to implying Q, so use them only when P is indeed true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'If P, then Q' from 'Since P, Q.' Ensure P is established before such linkage. Examples show proper/ improper usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Thus, hence, therefore' Correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: These adverbs should precede a statement that follows logically from previous statements; ensure the subsequent statement indeed follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: 'Therefore 2k+1.' Better: 'Therefore a = 2k + 1.' Always ensure logical consequence holds.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Taking Square Roots or Other Monotone Operations, Check Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: When applying monotone functions (e.g., square root) to both sides of an inequality, ensure hypotheses (such as positivity) that preserve the inequality direction are satisfied and cite earlier propositions if needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: After proving 4xy < (x+y)^2, one may take square roots to conclude 2√(xy) < x + y provided x,y>0, justified by a previous proposition about monotonicity of sqrt on positives.

rubrics_metrics.name: In Modular/Divisibility Proofs, Use the Definition n | (a-b)
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving congruence or divisibility statements, start from the definition (n | (a-b)) to produce an integer witness and manipulate algebraically (e.g., multiply both sides) to reach desired congruence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: From a ≡ b (mod n) write a - b = nk for some k ∈ Z, multiply by (a+b) to get a^2 - b^2 = n(k(a+b)), conclude a^2 ≡ b^2 (mod n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case Splitting on Sign/Parity/Size When Needed
rubrics_metrics.description: When properties depend on sign, parity, or relative size (e.g., a positive/zero/negative parameter), split into cases accordingly and construct witnesses (e.g., choose n depending on sign).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: representing any multiple of 4 as 1+(-1)^{2n-1} required separate handling of a=0, a>0, a<0 with explicit constructions for n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present Intermediate Steps Clearly (Avoid Omitted Steps Early On)
rubrics_metrics.description: Especially when learning, do not omit routine intermediate steps; present algebraic manipulations and justifications on separate lines for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes: 'One doesn't normally use a separate line for each sentence in a proof, but for clarity we will often do this in the first few chapters.' Follow this until comfortable.
